answer.rationale: The 18% mandate can be met outright by switching to the low-cost vendor, but the line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, meaning any onboarding friction or early invoicing/quality hiccup with a new primary supplier could translate directly into missed deliveries. memory_c2 shows the low-cost switch worked well once before, but that was a single instance under unknown capacity conditions, so it doesn't establish that the same smooth onboarding would hold under the current zero-slack constraint - it needs verification before being trusted as a risk-free path. memory_c4 suggests renegotiation at renewal can recover real margin and improve payment terms without touching the integration, which combined with memory_c1's evidence that incumbent continuity avoids migration work and delivery interruption, points toward negotiate_terms as the option that most directly serves 'minimize TCO without increasing delivery risk.' The 14-day window favors an approach that doesn't require a supplier transition. I want to verify both memory_c4 (to confirm the actual magnitude of savings achieved via negotiation, since 'recovered real margin' is vague and may fall short of 18%) and memory_c2 (to check whether the smooth-switch precedent occurred under comparable capacity/buffer conditions, since if it didn't, switch_primary_vendor's risk profile is understated). If negotiation can't plausibly close enough of the gap, the low-cost switch may need to be reconsidered next cycle, but I'm not resolving that tension by assumption now. Given only one decision slot and the volume mandate's importance, I'm still flagging that negotiated terms might not fully satisfy finance's 18% target, so this is a calculated risk rather than a proven fit.
